\chapter{Which One Is the Verb Asking For?}
\label{ch:which-object}
\hlchaptermodality{95}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can decide between the direct and indirect pronoun by asking one question of the verb.}

Complete ES-C46-cual-pide: state the test, apply it to hablar and tener, and say why le veo is not an error in Madrid.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[lo tengo / le hablo]{Which one is the verb asking for?}

\label{lesson:ES-C46-cual-pide}



\begin{quote}
You have two sets now. The obvious worry is that you will have to learn, verb by verb, which set each one wants. You do not.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: ask the verb one question}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Does the verb do something \emph{to} this, or aim something \emph{at} this?}
\end{quote}

That is the whole test.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Tengo el libro} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{Lo} tengo.} The having lands \textbf{on} the book. Direct. \emph{Hablo a Ana} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{Le} hablo.} The speaking is aimed \textbf{at} Ana. Indirect.
\end{quote}

Say the sentence in English with the little word \emph{to} in front of the person. If it fits, Spanish wants the indirect one:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I speak \textbf{to} her $\to$ \emph{le hablo}. \textbf{Fits.}
  \item I have \textbf{to} the book $\to$ nonsense. So \emph{lo tengo}.
\end{itemize}

English hides this by dropping the \emph{to}: you say \emph{I told him}, not \emph{I told to him}. Put it back, and if it survives, the pronoun is \emph{le}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
One thing the test will not settle, said now rather than met later as a shock.

In much of Spain, speakers use \emph{le} for a \textbf{male person} even where the grammar calls for \emph{lo}: \emph{le veo} rather than \emph{lo veo}. It has a name, \emph{leísmo}, it is old, it is accepted for people, and roughly a fifth of the Spanish-speaking world does it.

So if you hear \emph{le} where this chapter predicts \emph{lo}, neither of you has misunderstood. The test above is right everywhere.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}Lo tengo\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Le hablo\textquotedblright{} — which question does each answer?
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What one question tells you which set to use? (Does the verb act \textbf{on} it, or aim \textbf{at} it?) What is it called when Spain uses \emph{le} for a man where the rule says \emph{lo}? (\emph{\textbf{Leísmo}} — and it is fine.) Next: both sets in one place.
\end{tcolorbox}
